property_summary: Rule: When called by the current owner, setOwner(x) sets owner to the provided parameter x (i.e., owner() == x after the call); the mutant that assigns tx.origin breaks this because it ignores the provided parameter and sets owner to tx.origin instead.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(_owner) sets C.owner() equal to the provided _owner; the mutant that unconditionally sets owner = address(0) violates this by making owner() == address(0) for some fuzzed _owner values.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) updates the public owner state to _owner; the mutant that omits the assignment will leave owner unchanged for some inputs (when the caller is the current owner).

For any address caller that is equal to the current owner and any target address newOwner, calling setOwner(newOwner) results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant that omits the assignment can leave owner() unchanged for some (caller, newOwner) pairs where caller == initial owner.

For any caller address A and any target address T, when the reference C's setOwner(T) is invoked by A it succeeds iff A == C.owner(), so if it succeeds the contract's owner becomes T; the mutant inverts the guard so calls by the current owner are rejected and thus the owner does not update for those inputs (owner caller == current owner).

For any caller that is the current owner and any non-zero target address, calling setOwner(target) updates owner to target; the mutant wrongly leaves owner unchanged when target is address(0), so it violates that the owner is updated to the provided non-zero address (and additionally changes behavior for zero by preventing setting to zero when original allows it).

For every caller that is the current owner, calling setOwner(...) succeeds and returns true; the mutant changes the return value to false for some inputs, so the reference always returns true while the mutant can return false.

For any caller who is the current owner and any _owner argument, calling setOwner(...) on the correct contract always returns true (i.e., the external call completes and returns true); the mutant instead returns true only when the new owner is the zero address, so for non-zero _owner it will return false and violate the rule.

For any caller A who is the current owner and any address X provided as parameter, after calling setOwner(X) the contract's owner becomes X (the provided argument); the mutant that ignores X and sets owner to msg.sender breaks this rule for inputs where msg.sender != X.

For every input address X, calling setOwner(X) on the correct contract sets the public owner to exactly X (owner == X); the mutant that assigns payable(_owner) can change the stored value when types/addresses interact such that owner != X for some inputs (the mutant causes a mismatch between the passed address and the stored owner for some fuzzed addresses).

For any address candidate newOwner, calling setOwner(newOwner) as the current owner stores exactly newOwner in the public owner variable; the mutant that assigns payable(_owner) can change behavior for addresses where payable(...) produces a different value (e.g., when type conversion or truncated/address-mismatch occurs), so the mutant will sometimes make owner != newOwner.

For every address newOwner, when the current owner calls setOwner(newOwner) the stored owner getter equals the exact address value newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = payable(_owner) can change behavior for addresses that are contract addresses whose fallback/receive reverts on sending Ether (payable conversion itself doesn't send Ether but storing payable(address) vs address is identical — to provoke a difference we instead exploit that payable conversion may be misused only when subsequent balance-related semantics differ, so we assert that calling setOwner from the current owner always succeeds (does not revert) for any address input; the mutant will still succeed, but we widen to require that the call does not change address(c).balance (the correct contract never moves funds), while a modified version that involved transferring would change the balance), and so the test detects mutants that perform an unintended transfer.

For every address newOwner and call by the current owner, C.setOwner(newOwner) always sets the public owner getter to exactly newOwner (no funds are moved and no revert), while the mutant that stores a payable-converted address and may attempt value-related behavior will cause the post-call owner getter to differ for some inputs; the test asserts owner == newOwner after a successful call.

For any address newOwner and when called by the current owner, C.setOwner(newOwner) never changes contract balance and always stores exactly newOwner in the public owner getter; the mutant that assigns a payable-converted value and might perform value-related behaviour can differ on some inputs by changing address(c).balance or storing a different owner.

The owner can only be changed by transactions initiated directly by the current owner (msg.sender == owner); the mutant allowing tx.origin == owner lets a different caller (a contract called by the owner) change owner, so there exist inputs where owner differs after setOwner between reference and mutant.

For every caller X and newOwner Y, if X calls setOwner(Y) directly then the contract's owner becomes Y only when X equals the current owner (msg.sender==owner); the mutant that checks tx.origin instead allows a call initiated by a non-owner contract (where msg.sender != owner but tx.origin == owner) to change owner — so the rule: any direct call (no intermediate contracts) to setOwner results in owner == caller_after if and only if caller was the previous owner, which holds for the reference but can be violated by the mutant when a contract intermediary forwards the call.

For any addresses caller and newOwner, when the current owner directly calls setOwner(newOwner) the contract's owner becomes newOwner (reference guarantees only direct caller who equals owner can change owner); the mutant that uses tx.origin can be changed by an intermediate contract call where msg.sender != owner but tx.origin == owner, so there exist inputs (an intermediate contract address) that make the mutant's owner differ.

For any caller address, calling setOwner succeeds (returns / does not revert) when the caller equals the current owner; the mutant that changes the onlyOwner check to require(msg.sender == address(0)) will cause setOwner to revert for legitimate owner callers (non-zero), so the reference always allows the current owner to call setOwner but the mutant blocks those calls for many inputs.

For all callers, calling setOwner(x) on the correct contract C can only change owner when the caller is the current owner; the mutant removes this restriction so some non-owner caller can change owner.
